idiom_name: func Identity[T any](x T) T plus first-class func values / pass-through middleware
implementation_notes: Go's standard library has no polymorphic identity (no counterpart to Haskell's id or Java's Function.identity()), and before Go 1.18 an honest, type-preserving one was untypeable — an interface{}-based Id(x any) any erases the static type. Since type parameters (Go 1.18+), the canonical form is a one-line generic function func Identity[T any](x T) T { return x }, which is type-preserving by construction and instantiates per type argument into an ordinary non-generic function. The classic structure (a Strategy/Null-Object interface hierarchy for the 'do nothing' case) is replaced by Go's first-class func values: a declared func type such as Transformer[T any] func(T) T composes via ordinary loops with Identity as the fold base case, and in http middleware chains the neutral decorator is the pass-through func that returns its input handler unchanged (func(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return next }). A dedicated named type or struct is justified only when the neutral element must carry state or satisfy a broader interface; the compiler inlines trivial functions, so a direct Identity call adds no runtime cost.
pitfalls: An any-typed identity (func Id(x any) any — the pre-generics workaround) silently erases the static type: the return type is no longer the input type, every caller must type-assert the result back, and a wrong assertion panics at runtime — the type-preserving property is the whole point of the pattern.

A nil func value is not the identity: Go's zero value for a func type, field, or slot is nil, and calling through it panics; a pipeline slot that 'defaults to no-op' must be explicitly seeded with the identity function — nil does not mean pass-through.

Each distinct instantiation is a distinct function: Identity[int] is not assignable where Transformer[string] is expected (good — caught at the assignment site), but routing the value through an any parameter or a func(any) signature accepts anything and hides exactly the type/arity mismatch the generic signature was there to catch.

A pass-through closure defined in a loop that captures the loop variable (pre-Go 1.22 per-iteration semantics) observes the last element on every iteration — an 'identity' closure that does not return its input unchanged across iterations.

The compiler inlines trivial functions such as Identity, so a direct call is free — but storing func values in slices, structs, or interfaces allocates and the indirect call defeats inlining; profile before inserting identity indirection into a latency-critical loop.

Go's comparators (sort.Slice less funcs, slices.SortFunc with cmp.Compare) return bool or a three-way int, so the C-style binary identity (a, b) -> 0 has no direct Go form; when a natural ordering exists, sort the values directly instead of deriving a key through a forced identity extractor.
